title: Dalit Christians
hook: Indian Christians from communities once called untouchable

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antioch, where the name was first spoken, and your line was the oldest churches.

Who is allowed to touch whom? Societies keep quiet rules about it, and children pick them up early. In Mark's Gospel a man with a skin disease, a leper, kneels in the road in front of Jesus. By the custom of the day, people kept their distance from him, and he kept his from them. He says, if you want to, you can make me clean. And before Jesus says a word in reply, he does what everyone else had been careful not to do. He reaches out and touches him.

In India, caste has divided people for a long time, and at the bottom of that order were communities treated as untouchable: kept from wells, from temples, from the tables of others. Dalit is a name people from these communities use for themselves today. Among India's Christians are Dalit families, and some of them heard their own story in that leper on the road. Mark tells it like this, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." Touch first, then words. Paul wrote something just as plain: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." But caste did not stop at the church door. Dalit Christians and church leaders in India have spoken about separate seating, separate cemeteries, and pulpits closed to them in some places, inside the church itself. So some Dalit Christian thinkers read the Bible from where they stood, and called it Dalit theology. They noticed that Jesus himself was pushed out, and read Isaiah's line about the servant as their own: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." On that reading, God isn't at the top of the ladder looking down, but with the ones the ladder left out. Churches in India are still working out what that asks of them.

segments.voice: Think of someone you see often but never really greet: the person who cleans the office, the one who brings your packages, the relative everyone talks over at dinner, and notice whether you know their name. Hold that face with the respect you'd give someone you admire. If you pray, pray for them by name, or by face if that's all you have; if not, simply wish them well.
Dalit Christians. Indian Christians from communities once treated as untouchable, and a theology that reads the Gospel from the bottom of the ladder.
Your line: no one untouchable. On the road, the touch came before the words. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Dalit Christian communities in India worship in their own congregations and in mixed ones, and churches and Dalit theologians have taken up the fight against caste discrimination, including within the church.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'many Indian Christians' was cut (no cited count); the hook field now reads 'Indian Christians from communities once called untouchable' and the script says only 'Among India's Christians are Dalit families'. Keeper may restore if a source is cited.
Caste is described as an Indian social order without attributing it to any religion, to avoid framing the Hindu path as a foil. Confirm the wording is fair.
'Dalit is a name people from these communities use for themselves today': no etymology given. Confirm.
Discrimination inside churches (separate seating, cemeteries, barriers to ordination/pulpits) is documented by Indian church bodies and Dalit theologians; stated as 'in some places'. Confirm.
Dalit theology's reading of Isaiah 53 and of Jesus as rejected (e.g. Arvind Nirmal, James Massey; not named): confirm the summary.
'By the custom of the day, people kept their distance from him': based on Leviticus 13:45–46; kept general to avoid casting Jewish law as a foil. Confirm.
